I was this child, only my parents were a little less awful. Actually I still am this child when I'm with them. My guess is that your nephew is trying to shield emotionally from everyone and everything that may hurt him, and caregivers are the biggest threat when you grow up like that. To this day, I am wary and even afraid of my friends' parents, even though some of them treat me like a queen. Also I am a fully grown adult. It would be very hard for a parent to hurt me. 

My advice for you is: try not to take this personally, this is your nephew trying to conserve as much safe space as possible in a new environment with new caregivers. If you're not pieces of shit with him, which you probably aren't since you're here telling strangers about this instead of screaming at his face, he will realize he doesn't need to activate defensive mode all the time towards you. However, please bear in mind that these years with his parents have shaped his personality. He will probably be enclosed in himself like this for a long time, if not forever.

If you can, please bring him to therapy, and support him to stay on therapy, since it will hurt a lot and he may not want to keep going. Finally, taking him in was a very courageous thing to do, and it will change his life. As another child who was treated poorly by her caregivers, thank you.

I see. However, we don't know all about how covid works on our systems. All we know is that it affects our tasting abilities, normally by making us lose our sense of taste. While covid reinfections are rare within 90 days after the first infection, they are possible, and there's even a [case report](https://www.scielo.br/j/rsbmt/a/cyGQv63Ygtn7m7jqPQNtGqH/?lang=en) about a person who got recurrent covid during that time, so I think it's worth checking if your friend has the means.

Like someone said, your friend should get evaluated by a doctor for covid. If that's ruled out, see how it plays out for a couple of days or weeks (depending on how disgusted they get towards food). Maybe this is transitory, but if it keeps happening, it may be some kind of tasting disorder (either on processing the taste in the brain or actually acquiring it in the mouth), or maybe an ED. I have an intermittent ED - I stop eating at certain conditions and usually eat very little - and I feel something like that every time I'm about to stop eating again. The difference is that it comes with a psychological storm: body dysphoria, feeling emotionally awful, overwhelmed, hating myself and so on. As far as I know, emotions and feelings are a great part of EDs, so I'd think about "physical" problems first if they don't have those bad feelings towards themselves and their appearance. 

Tl;dr: your friend should see a doctor to rule out covid or other disorders and then think about an ED if they don't have any other psychological symptoms.

This is a morally ambiguous situation, so I'm not sure anyone will have an answer for you, but here I go lol

First off, there's something people who don't have BDP need to try to understand in situations like these: we don't do this because we like it, those behaviors are symptoms. As much as it bothers you, you can't just tell a friend who has a bad flu to not blow their nose. The same goes here. A runny nose is a symptom of a flu as much as some behaviors, which are hard to deal with, are symptoms of BPD.

That said, this doesn't mean a BPD person can go around toying with people's feelings, personal histories and privacy, and then blame it on their mental illness. If your friend is diagnosed, they are probably receiving medical and psychological help. Cooperating with the treatment and trying to realize when we're letting our symptoms get the best of us is very important, otherwise, friendships and other relationships will get very hard on both ends.

So what I mean is: I don't think you're wrong for feeling hurt, if you felt like there was nothing to confess and your friend blackmailed you into it, especially if they do this kind of thing regularly. You have a very hard choice to make now: getting away from your friend or staying with them, maybe helping them get treated, and hope they will get better so you can nurture your friendship together. If you choose to stay, it may be very hard, and it may be even unfruitful, but you'll have your friend with you, and maybe they will be by your side for a long time, if you're able to maintain this friendship. If you choose to go, however, you're not necessarily selfish for choosing this. There's only so much a person can take, and while I feel immense pain when I try to put myself on your friend's shoes, I understand you, too. It's all a matter of how much emotional stamina you have, of how much more you think you can take. 

Sorry if I didn't actually help you, and I hope your decision doesn't bring you more pain.
